 Banks Lift Deposit Rates After RBI Hike, Lending Costs Rise 
 Banks Lift Deposit Rates After RBI Hike, Lending Costs Rise
 BW Online Bureau
 Nov 12, 2026
 # Banking 
 # RBI 
 # Interest Rates 
 # Fixed Deposits 
 # Bank Deposits 
 # Lending Rates 
 # Monetary Policy 
 # Personal Finance 
 Lenders raise fixed deposit returns on select maturities as higher funding costs and inflation above the RBI's tolerance ceiling begin to feed into borrowing rates
 Gallery
 Indian banks are raising fixed deposit (FD) rates and increasing lending benchmarks following the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 25-basis-point repo rate hike in October. The repricing, which has gathered pace in November, is pushing up returns for depositors while gradually increasing borrowing costs for customers. 
 The rate revisions span public and private sector lenders, with banks offering higher interest on selected deposit tenures rather than across their entire deposit portfolios. At the same time, seven major lenders have raised their marginal cost of funds-based lending rates (MCLR) by 5-20 basis points across selected tenures in October and November, signalling the transmission of tighter monetary conditions to bank lending. 
 Deposit Rates Move Higher Across Banks 
State-owned Bank of Baroda revised rates on its special 555-day bob Golden Goal Deposit Scheme by 10 basis points, effective Thursday. The maximum interest rate has risen to 7.50 per cent, with the revised rates applying to retail term deposits below Rs 3 crore. Rates on other deposit maturities remain unchanged. 
 For general customers, the bank is offering 6.85 per cent on callable deposits and 6.90 per cent on non-callable deposits. Resident senior citizens can earn up to 7.40 per cent, while super senior citizens aged 80 years and above are eligible for rates of up to 7.50 per cent. 
 Federal Bank has also raised the additional interest benefit for senior citizens on term deposits to 0.60 per cent from 0.50 per cent. The revision, effective Thursday, takes the maximum interest rate on select maturities to 7.50 per cent. It applies to deposits with tenures of 18 months and two years to less than three years. 
 Senior citizens will earn 7.40 per cent on deposits with a premature withdrawal facility and 7.50 per cent on deposits of Rs 1 crore and above without the facility. The bank has indicated that the effective annualised yield on these deposits could reach 8.18 per cent and 8.30 per cent, respectively, for a 35-month tenure. General customers, including non-resident Indians, will earn 6.80 per cent and 6.90 per cent on the respective deposit options. 
 Private And Public Sector Banks Revise FD Rates 
The revisions extend beyond the two lenders, with several banks adjusting rates on selected maturities and special deposit schemes in recent weeks. Among private sector lenders, HDFC Bank has raised FD rates by up to 50 basis points on select tenures, while ICICI Bank has increased rates by 10 basis points on selected longer-term deposits. Kotak Mahindra Bank's revisions have taken its highest rate for general customers to 6.80 per cent. 
 Public sector lenders have also adjusted their deposit offerings. Canara Bank has raised rates by up to 15 basis points on selected tenures, including its 555-day deposit. Indian Overseas Bank increased the rate on its 444-day deposit by 15 basis points to 6.75 per cent. 
 Indian Bank has revised rates on its special 555-day and 777-day deposit schemes by 15 basis points each, taking them to 6.80 per cent and 6.75 per cent, respectively. Small finance banks are offering higher rates to attract deposits. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is offering up to 8.50 per cent to senior citizens, while Suryoday Small Finance Bank's highest rate for the segment stands at 8.60 per cent. 
 Lending Rates Begin To Reflect Higher Funding Costs 
The repricing is also extending to the lending side. State Bank of India (SBI), HDFC Bank, Punjab National Bank, Bank of India, Indian Bank, Canara Bank and Bank of Baroda have increased their marginal cost of funds-based lending rates (MCLR) by 5-20 basis points across selected tenures during October and November. 
 MCLR is a benchmark used by banks to determine interest rates on certain floating-rate loans. An increase in the benchmark can raise borrowing costs for customers whose loans are linked to MCLR, depending on the applicable reset period and loan terms. The October policy decision raised the RBI's repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent and shifted its monetary policy stance to calibrated tightening. The central bank's decision came amid concerns over inflationary pressures and global uncertainties.
